input:
This cost review examines the annual transport cost associated with a cross-dock transfer operation. The route in question involves 579 km per trip, charged at a rate of $1.98 per km, and the operation runs a total of 890 trips per year. When these components are brought together, the annual transport cost comes to $1020k, making transport a significant element of the overall cost picture for the operation. The figures are drawn from carrier invoices for the last 12 months, so they reflect the charges that have actually been incurred over that period rather than any estimated or budgeted amounts.

It is important to note that empty running is included in the trip count, which means that the trips that have been counted are all of the trips that the carrier invoiced, whether they were loaded or running empty. The annual figure therefore represents the cost of running the transfer operation as a whole, and it should not be interpreted as the cost of the loaded movement on its own. Indeed, a cost per loaded kilometre calculated from these figures would come out higher than the headline rate might suggest, precisely because the empty trips add distance and cost without carrying any load. For this reason, any comparison with an alternative routing or an alternative carrier needs to be carried out on a like-for-like basis, with all trips counted, in order to ensure that the comparison is a fair one.
target:
Annual transport cost for the cross-dock transfer is $1020k. The figure is built up from the operation's three components: 579 km per trip, at $1.98 per km, over 890 trips per year. It is a restatement of the carrier invoices for the last 12 months, which are the cost base of the review: the components are the invoiced distance, the invoiced rate and the invoiced trip count, so the annual figure is a measured cost for the year in question and not an estimate built from budgeted rates or assumed mileages.

Empty running is included in the trip count: the trips counted are all the trips the carrier invoiced, loaded and empty alike. The annual cost is therefore the cost of the transfer operation as a whole, and not the cost of the loaded movement alone. A cost per loaded kilometre drawn from these figures would stand higher than the invoiced rate, because the empty trips add distance and charge while carrying no load, and the loaded kilometres over which the total is spread are fewer than the kilometres on which the total was incurred.

Any comparison of the transfer against an alternative routing or an alternative carrier has to be made on the same basis, with all trips counted. A comparison that counted loaded trips only would credit the alternative with an efficiency the present operation's figures do not claim, and the saving it appeared to show would be an artefact of the counting rather than a property of the alternative.
